explanations.explanation: Jerusalem it is, friend. The verse says that at Perga, John left them “to return to Jerusalem” (Acts 13:13). It doesn't tell us why, so I'm not going to make something up. All we know is the team is one helper lighter, and the rest of them keep moving.

Tarsus doesn't show up on this trip, friend. The verse says John left them at Perga “to return to Jerusalem” (Acts 13:13). So he heads back to Jerusalem while Paul and the others keep going. Don't worry about the map. I once got lost walking from my oven to my cookie box, and that's FOUR steps.

Joppa's not where this road goes, friend. John left them at Perga “to return to Jerusalem” (Acts 13:13). One helper peels off, and the rest keep traveling. Hold on to that name John, because Paul is going to mention a different John later, and I don't want you mixing them up like I mix up my sprinkle jars.

Yes sir! In Pisidian Antioch, they “entered the synagogue on the Sabbath and sat down” (Acts 13:14). After that long trip inland from Perga, I'd sit down too. Shoot, I'd sit down and ask for a pillow. But they're not just resting, friend. Sitting in that synagogue puts them right where the next thing happens.

It's true, friend. After the trip inland from Perga, they “entered the synagogue on the Sabbath and sat down” (Acts 13:14). Think about it. You walk ALL that way, you find the synagogue, and you take a seat. That's exactly what they do, and that seat is about to turn into a pulpit.

Encouragement, friend! The synagogue leaders send word, “Brothers, if you have a word of encouragement for the people, please speak” (Acts 13:15). They read from the Law and the Prophets, then they open the floor to the visitors. That's an open mic, and Paul is about to take it.

The leaders ask for something sweeter than a warning, friend. They say, “Brothers, if you have a word of encouragement for the people, please speak” (Acts 13:15). That's a kind invitation right after the reading from the Law and the Prophets. Nobody walks up to a guest and says, “Hey, scare us a little.”

Close neighborhood, different house, friend. The Prophets were just read, but the leaders ask for a word of encouragement: “Brothers, if you have a word of encouragement for the people, please speak” (Acts 13:15). They invite the visitors to say something that builds the people up. And Paul does NOT need to be asked twice.

True! Paul says of God, “He endured their conduct for about forty years in the wilderness” (Acts 13:18). Forty years, friend. I lose patience waiting forty SECONDS for my oven to preheat. God's patience with His people is a whole different level.

It's true, friend. Paul says of God, “He endured their conduct for about forty years in the wilderness” (Acts 13:18). That's Paul walking through Israel's history, and this part is about God's patience. About forty years of it, out in the wilderness.

A king, friend. Paul says, “Then the people asked for a king,” and God gave them Saul son of Kish (Acts 13:21). They've had judges, they've had Samuel the prophet, and now they want a crown on somebody. And God answers that request.

The people ask for a king, friend. Paul says, “Then the people asked for a king,” and God gave them Saul son of Kish from the tribe of Benjamin (Acts 13:21). Paul's history moves from judges to kings here. A building isn't part of this step of the story.

They already had a prophet, friend! God gave them judges “until the time of Samuel the prophet” (Acts 13:20). Then “the people asked for a king,” and God gave them Saul (Acts 13:21). Asking for a prophet when Samuel's standing right there is like me asking for a cookie stamper. Friend, I AM the cookie stamper.

David, friend! After removing Saul, God “raised up David as their king” and called him “a man after My own heart” (Acts 13:22). And keep your eye on David, because Paul isn't done with him. He's about to connect David to the Savior.

The crown goes outside Saul's house, friend. Paul says that after removing Saul, God “raised up David as their king” (Acts 13:22). God testified that David son of Jesse is “a man after My own heart” (Acts 13:22). Jonathan isn't mentioned in Paul's sermon at all.

Samuel's a prophet, not the king here, friend. Paul places Samuel at the end of the time of the judges (Acts 13:20). Then, after removing Saul, God “raised up David as their king” (Acts 13:22). Samuel's in the history, but David gets the crown.

Sandals! John says, “But there is One coming after me whose sandals I am not worthy to untie” (Acts 13:25). That's the lowest job there is, untying somebody's dusty sandals, and John says he's not even worthy of THAT. That's humility, friend. And the One he's talking about is Jesus.

Lower than the belt, friend. All the way down to the feet. John says, “But there is One coming after me whose sandals I am not worthy to untie” (Acts 13:25). He's saying he's not even worthy of the dustiest little task for the One coming after him, and that One is Jesus.

Look down, friend, way down. John says, “But there is One coming after me whose sandals I am not worthy to untie” (Acts 13:25). Untying sandals is about the humblest job around, and John says even that is too high for him. The One coming after him is Jesus.

They found nothing, friend. Paul says, “And though they found no ground for a death sentence, they asked Pilate to have Him executed” (Acts 13:28). No ground. Not a crumb of a reason. And they still went to Pilate to have Him executed.

False is right. Paul says, “And though they found no ground for a death sentence, they asked Pilate to have Him executed” (Acts 13:28). Let that sink in, friend. They had NOTHING on Him, and they still asked for His death.

That tomb was not His forever address, friend. Paul says it plain: “But God raised Him from the dead” (Acts 13:30). They laid Him in a tomb (Acts 13:29), and God raised Him. That's the turning point of Paul's whole sermon.

False! After they laid Him in a tomb (Acts 13:29), Paul says, “But God raised Him from the dead” (Acts 13:30). That “But God” is my favorite little phrase, friend. Everything was going one way, and then BUT GOD.

explanations.answer: Those who came with Him from Galilee
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend! Paul says He was seen “by those who had accompanied Him from Galilee to Jerusalem” (Acts 13:31). And those people are “now His witnesses to our people” (Acts 13:31). They walked with Him, they saw Him alive again, and now they tell it.

explanations.answer: The rulers who condemned Him in Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: Not the rulers, friend. Paul says those rulers didn't even recognize Jesus (Acts 13:27). After God raised Him, He was seen “by those who had accompanied Him from Galilee to Jerusalem” (Acts 13:31). The ones who walked with Him are the ones who saw Him, and now they're His witnesses.

explanations.answer: The synagogue leaders of Pisidian Antioch
explanations.explanation: These folks are hearing about it from Paul, friend, not seeing it themselves. Paul says Jesus was seen “by those who had accompanied Him from Galilee to Jerusalem” (Acts 13:31). The leaders in Antioch are the ones who asked for a word of encouragement (Acts 13:15). And boy, are they getting one.

Jesus, friend! Paul says, “But the One whom God raised from the dead did not see decay” (Acts 13:37). David served, died and saw decay (Acts 13:36), so that Psalm about the Holy One can't be about David. It's about Jesus, the Savior God brought to Israel (Acts 13:23). That's Paul connecting the dots like a pro.

Paul's point is about One person, friend, and it's not Samuel. He says, “But the One whom God raised from the dead did not see decay” (Acts 13:37). That's Jesus. David saw decay (Acts 13:36), but the One God raised did not.

explanations.answer: Saul son of Kish from Benjamin
explanations.explanation: Saul's not the one Paul's pointing to here, friend. Paul says David saw decay (Acts 13:36), “But the One whom God raised from the dead did not see decay” (Acts 13:37). God raised Jesus from the dead (Acts 13:30). So the Psalm's Holy One is Jesus.

Moses, friend! Paul says that through Jesus “everyone who believes is justified from everything from which you could not be justified by the law of Moses” (Acts 13:39). Everything, friend. EVERYTHING. What the law couldn't do for them, Jesus does for everyone who believes.

Abraham's in the sermon, but not in this line, friend. Paul calls them “children of Abraham” (Acts 13:26), but the law he names is the law of Moses (Acts 13:39). Through Jesus, everyone who believes is justified from everything the law of Moses couldn't justify them from. That's the good news Paul is preaching.

David gets a LOT of airtime in this sermon, so I see why you went there, friend. But the law Paul names is “the law of Moses” (Acts 13:39). Through Jesus, everyone who believes is justified from everything that law couldn't justify them from. David's the king, Moses is the law.

Scoffers it is. Paul quotes the prophets: “Look, you scoffers, wonder and perish!” (Acts 13:41). Then comes the kicker, friend. God says He's doing a work in their days that they would never believe, even if someone told them. Paul ends his sermon with a warning: don't let that be you (Acts 13:40).

No idols in this warning, friend. Paul quotes the prophets: “Look, you scoffers, wonder and perish!” (Acts 13:41). It's aimed at people who hear about God's work and refuse to believe it. Paul's warning to his listeners is to watch out that this doesn't happen to them (Acts 13:40).

It's the scoffers, friend. Paul quotes, “Look, you scoffers, wonder and perish!” (Acts 13:41). These are folks who wouldn't believe God's work even if someone told them. That's me with a new cookie recipe. “That'll never work.” Then it works, and I look silly.

explanations.answer: Continue this message on the next Sabbath
explanations.explanation: You got it, friend. The people urged them “to continue this message on the next Sabbath” (Acts 13:42). They want MORE. Paul just preached a whole sermon, and the crowd says, “Do it again next week.” That's the best review a preacher can get.

explanations.answer: Leave the city before the next Sabbath
explanations.explanation: The opposite, friend! The people urged them “to continue this message on the next Sabbath” (Acts 13:42). They aren't showing Paul and Barnabas the door. They're asking for a part two.

explanations.answer: Write this message down for the leaders
explanations.explanation: They want to HEAR it again, friend. The people urged them “to continue this message on the next Sabbath” (Acts 13:42). Nobody asks for a written copy. They want Paul back in person next week, and that's a sign the message landed.

Grace, friend! Paul and Barnabas urged them “to continue in the grace of God” (Acts 13:43). They just heard that through Jesus the forgiveness of sins is proclaimed (Acts 13:38). Now the word is: keep standing right there in that grace.

Paul just finished saying the law of Moses couldn't justify them from everything (Acts 13:39), friend. So he points them somewhere better. Paul and Barnabas urged them “to continue in the grace of God” (Acts 13:43). Grace is where they're told to stay.

Not the house, friend, the grace. Paul and Barnabas urged them “to continue in the grace of God” (Acts 13:43). It's not about which building they stand in. It's about staying in God's grace that they just heard about through Jesus (Acts 13:38-39).

Jealousy, friend. When the Jews saw the crowds, “they were filled with jealousy” (Acts 13:45). Nearly the whole city shows up, and instead of joy, it's jealousy. I couldn't get three bakers to a taste test, and even I wouldn't be jealous of THAT crowd. Okay, maybe a little.

Funny, “wonder” was in Paul's warning about scoffers (Acts 13:41). But here, when the Jews saw the crowds, “they were filled with jealousy” (Acts 13:45). And it doesn't stay quiet, friend. They start contradicting what Paul is saying.

It's jealousy, friend. When the Jews saw the crowds, “they were filled with jealousy” (Acts 13:45). Nearly the whole city gathered to hear the word of the Lord (Acts 13:44). Not everyone is happy about that, and it shows.
The Gentiles! Paul and Barnabas say, “we now turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13:46). They spoke the word to the Jews first, like they said they had to. Now the door swings wide open, friend. WIDE open.

They're not heading back to Jerusalem, friend. Paul and Barnabas say, “we now turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13:46). Those Jews in Antioch rejected the word, so the message goes to the Gentiles. And the Gentiles are right there listening.

Tarsus never comes up here, friend. Paul and Barnabas say, “we now turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13:46). It's not about one city. It's about a whole group of people who are about to hear the word of God.

The ends of the earth! The Lord's words go, “I have made you a light for the Gentiles, to bring salvation to the ends of the earth” (Acts 13:47). Friend, I've got one little cookie planet, and I still lose things on it. The Lord's talking about the whole EARTH, all the way to the edges.

Close, friend, but the word is ends. The Lord says, “I have made you a light for the Gentiles, to bring salvation to the ends of the earth” (Acts 13:47). Same big idea: salvation going as far as the earth goes. Paul and Barnabas say this is what the Lord commanded them.

The word is ends, friend. The Lord says, “I have made you a light for the Gentiles, to bring salvation to the ends of the earth” (Acts 13:47). The Gentiles are already named in the first half. The second half sends salvation as far as the earth goes.

explanations.answer: They celebrate and praise the Lord's message
explanations.explanation: Party in Pisidian Antioch! When the Gentiles heard this, “they rejoiced and glorified the word of the Lord” (Acts 13:48). They just heard the door is open for them, friend. You'd better believe they're celebrating.

explanations.answer: They hesitate and ask for a sign first
explanations.explanation: No hesitating here, friend. When the Gentiles heard this, “they rejoiced and glorified the word of the Lord” (Acts 13:48). They don't ask for a sign. They hear the message and they CELEBRATE.

explanations.answer: They go quiet and wait for their leaders
explanations.explanation: Quiet? Not even close, friend. When the Gentiles heard this, “they rejoiced and glorified the word of the Lord” (Acts 13:48). Nobody's waiting around for permission. They're rejoicing right then and there.

It gets out, friend! The verse says, “And the word of the Lord spread throughout that region” (Acts 13:49). Not just the city. The whole region. Kind of like when I sneak one cookie and somehow the whole bakery knows before the next batch is out.
False! “And the word of the Lord spread throughout that region” (Acts 13:49). One synagogue sermon, then nearly the whole city, and now the whole region. Friend, that message is MOVING.

explanations.answer: They are driven out of the district
explanations.explanation: Driven out, friend. They “stirred up persecution against Paul and Barnabas and drove them out of their district” (Acts 13:50). One Sabbath nearly the whole city shows up, and then they get pushed out of the district. But hold on, because they're not done.

explanations.answer: They are locked in the city jail
explanations.explanation: No jail in this verse, friend. They “stirred up persecution against Paul and Barnabas and drove them out of their district” (Acts 13:50). Nobody locks them up here. They push them out.

explanations.answer: They are sent back to Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: Nobody ships them to Jerusalem, friend. They “stirred up persecution against Paul and Barnabas and drove them out of their district” (Acts 13:50). They're driven out, and their road leads somewhere else entirely.

Iconium! They “shook the dust off their feet in protest against them and went to Iconium” (Acts 13:51). Driven out of one district, and they just keep walking. Friend, I get winded going from my oven to my cookie box. These two get chased out and go to the NEXT town.

Their next stop is Iconium, friend. The verse says they “shook the dust off their feet in protest against them and went to Iconium” (Acts 13:51). Shake off the dust, pick up the feet, head to Iconium.

It's Iconium, friend. They “shook the dust off their feet in protest against them and went to Iconium” (Acts 13:51). Chased out of one place, they don't sit and sulk. They brush off their feet and keep going.
